profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
profiles.judgment: Required first-year academic/personal development; not Dutch disciplinary methods.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: Required PPD

profiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
profiles.actualContent: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
profiles.judgment: Data cleaning, text/table/spatial manipulation and visualisation. Useful general methods, not a documented Dutch corpus-linguistics sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops data cleaning, visualisation and analysis, including text data

profiles.name: Modern History
profiles.actualContent: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
profiles.judgment: Modern political/economic world and European history; context, not Dutch literary history before/after1800.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides specific modern historical context for interpreting cultural texts and public discourse

profiles.name: History of Empires
profiles.actualContent: This course is about great powers, superpowers and even hyperpowers. ‘Empire’ is a powerful and dangerous word. It has a rich and ambiguous history and strong polemical connotations now and in the past. The typical empire is usually presented as oppressive and ruthless, although some of the modern empires are democracies that focus upon the improvements of its society. This course deals with some of the most important empires in World History. Next to this some of the most important theories on empires will be treated. How is the rise and fall of empires explained? What are the sources of empire and how are great power politics conducted?
profiles.judgment: Empires and theories of power; meaningful context for literature/power, not Dutch literary historiography.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines empire and power as specific historical contexts for cultural production and identity

profiles.name: History Research Seminar
profiles.actualContent: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
profiles.judgment: Actual primary-source research on the1809Walcheren expedition, including Dutch/French/British context. Genuine historical research, not a Dutch literary/linguistic thesis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops source criticism and a substantial research paper through historical inquiry

profiles.name: Philosophy of Mind
profiles.actualContent: o What is the nature of consciousness? o What explains the identity of selves over time? How have different philosophical traditions thought about this issue? o Can the mind be explained in neurobiological terms? o Are large language models conscious? Can they ever be? o What can we learn from dream states about conscious experience? o What can perceptual illusions teach us about our awareness of the world? o What are the differences between human and animal consciousness? These are some of the questions explored in the philosophy of mind, an important field of philosophy since early modernity. The field has come to prominence and maturation in the past decades alongside advances in the scientific study of the human mind, research on animal minds, and innovations in computing. In this course, we will focus both on important work from the history of the field and on contributions from recent scholarship. We shall begin with exploration of the nature of selves and personal identity, looking at historical sources in the Western tradition, contemporary debate, as well as the theory of the self in Buddhist thought. Detailed discussion of approaches to the mind-body problem, a key issue in the philosophy of mind, will follow. Additional topics to be examined in the course include: the possibility of intelligent and conscious machines, animal minds, dream states, the significance of transformative experiences, and the impact of novel technologies on the ways we experience the world.
profiles.judgment: Mind, consciousness, selves and related philosophy; not cultural philosophy specifically for Dutch studies.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines mind, consciousness, identity and their relation to brain and technology

profiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
profiles.actualContent: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
profiles.judgment: General sociological concepts/institutions and theory; contextual, not linguistic interaction analysis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides social theories and methods for analysing institutions, identity, inequality and interaction

profiles.name: Modern Sociology
profiles.actualContent: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
profiles.judgment: Modern social theory, imperialism and modernity; contextual, not Dutch sociolinguistics.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies modernity, imperialism and colonial responses through social theory

profiles.name: Neurobiology
profiles.actualContent: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.
profiles.judgment: Neurobiology, animal models, microscopy and brain anatomy. Broad cognitive foundation, not Dutch phonology/morphology.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides neurobiological foundations for the study of language and cognition

profiles.name: Perception & Action
profiles.actualContent: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
profiles.judgment: Neural perception/action; limited cognition contribution, not language-specific structure or history.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies neural mechanisms of sensory processing, perception and action

profiles.name: Higher Order Functions
profiles.actualContent: This course builds upon the knowledge gained in the introductory course in Cognitive Science. It will deepen your knowledge of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Also, your knowledge of experimental approaches in the field of cognitive neuroscience will be enhanced; such that you become able to evaluate research findings and to design your own experiments. A selected number of higher order cognitive processes will be dealt with, including memory, emotion, social cognition, attention, consciousness, decision making and planning. In addition to established knowledge, current research questions will be discussed in depth.
profiles.judgment: Memory, attention, emotion and higher cognition with research design; contextual, not language-specific Dutch linguistics.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: deepens neurophysiology and studies higher cognition including language, memory and social cognition

profiles.name: Psycholinguistics
profiles.actualContent: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
profiles.judgment: Actual acquisition, bilingualism, speech comprehension, reading/dyslexia and experimental psycholinguistics. Strong genuine overlap, but not Dutch language history, phonology/morphology/syntax or advanced Dutch corpus studies.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: directly studies language acquisition, comprehension, production, bilingualism and language impairments through cognitive neuroscience

profiles.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
profiles.actualContent: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16
profiles.judgment: Brain/behaviour and psychology gateway; supports cognition, not a Dutch-studies foundation.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories that support later study of language processing

profiles.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
profiles.actualContent: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
profiles.judgment: Multivariate statistical models and APA reporting; useful quantitative support, not the full humanities hermeneutic/corpus/experimental methods sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops experimental design and advanced statistical analysis for behavioural evidence

profiles.name: Advanced Research Seminar
profiles.actualContent: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
profiles.judgment: Systematic review/meta-analysis inR; genuine research synthesis, not a guaranteed Dutch literary/linguistic individual thesis.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops systematic-review and meta-analytic methods for research synthesis

profiles.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
profiles.actualContent: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
profiles.judgment: Lifespan development, including language-related developmental context; not focused first-language acquisition or Dutch-as-second-language teaching.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines cognitive, biological and social development across the lifespan

profiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
profiles.actualContent: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
profiles.judgment: Rhetoric, argument and academic/public speaking: strong genuine communication foundation without Dutch-specific disciplinary depth.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: directly develops rhetorical analysis, persuasive writing and speaking

profiles.name: Dutch
profiles.actualContent: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
profiles.judgment: Actual beginner Dutch for uncomplicated daily speaking/writing and culture. Not native/advanced academic Dutch, Dutch linguistics or Dutch/Flemish literary history.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: provides basic everyday Dutch and cultural orientation without being presented as academic Dutch linguistics or proficiency

profiles.name: Style & Meaning
profiles.actualContent: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
profiles.judgment: Stylistic analysis of literary/nonfictional language, from phonetic to discourse/cognitive choices. Genuine textual analysis, not systematic Dutch phonology/morphology/syntax.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: analyses how linguistic choices create meaning, obligation, uncertainty and ideology in literary and non-fiction texts

profiles.name: Rhetoric in Action
profiles.actualContent: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
profiles.judgment: Real primary-school rhetoric teaching, mainly inDutch, with children9–12. Genuine applied communication and educational experience, not Dutch philology or a professional teaching qualification.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: applies rhetorical theory and public speaking with primary-school pupils, not Dutch subject teaching

profiles.name: Persuasive Communication
profiles.actualContent: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
profiles.judgment: Persuasion, framing/nudging, ethics and community communication projects. Genuine rhetoric/communication relevance, not a full Dutch public-debate or journalism qualification.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: applies ethical persuasion models to public communication about water, food and energy

profiles.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
profiles.actualContent: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
profiles.judgment: Poetry, performance, close reading, cultural theory and independent creative practice. Genuine literary craft; no specific Dutch/Flemish corpus or publishing/performance career guarantee.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies and practises poetic form, voice, sonic expression and performance

profiles.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
profiles.actualContent: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
profiles.judgment: Practical criticism, genres and literary interpretation. Strong genuine literary foundation; not a Dutch-specific literary sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: directly teaches practical literary interpretation across fiction, poetry, drama and narrative forms

profiles.name: Great Literary Works
profiles.actualContent: This course is based on a selection of major literary texts which should be considered essential for every LAS student’s cultural capital: texts that for centuries have inspired Western culture, visual arts and theatre, and which resonate themes that preoccupy social sciences and philosophy. The course is a chronological overview of literature ranging from the earliest monuments (the epic of Gilgamesh) to post-modernity. Within this framework students will read primary (literary) and secondary (critical, theoretical) texts debating what it means to be human, mortal, female, male, or child, or what it means to be responsible, free, a member of family or other community, to be civilized or barbarian. What makes literature different from anecdote? Why are some children’s texts indebted to philosophical tale? Probing these and many other questions, students will be invited to analyse literary representations of home, labour, leisure, duty, love, leadership, organized religion, and memory, and try to correlate these topics with various artistic forms used by writers. In this way the course is an encounter with diverse genres: heroic epic, philosophical tale, fairy tale, short story, autobiography, essay and novella. With this broad approach to themes and forms in the Western literary heritage, the course is an alternative introduction to literary studies, and of fundamental value to everyone interested in literary and cultural studies.
profiles.judgment: Broad world/Western literary history and primary texts. Strong literature contribution without sustained Dutch/Flemish history before and after1800.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: surveys literary forms and historical traditions while developing close reading across periods

profiles.name: World Myth & Literature
profiles.actualContent: How do ancient literary myths compare to the literature of other parts of the world? What can these parallels tell us about age-old global connections, or even about universal human themes? This course explores what might be tentatively named the literary silk road, but also taps into the narrative traditions of continents beyond. For instance, we investigate the similarities between the stories of ancient epic poems, from Homer to Virgil, with the Indian epic Mahabharata; we look at the strands between the romance novels of the classical world and those from Byzantine and Arabic literature. We explore how storytelling is expressed beyond text, for instance in oral traditions, visual culture, or in theatrical performance. The tradition of depicting mythical narratives is common to cultures all over the world. What are the processes of transmitting text into image? How do these literary images differ across cultures? Spanning four millennia and at least three continents, this course will examine how literary stories of myth form a deep cultural foundation, and how they deal with universal human themes like love, loyalty, power, and friendship.
profiles.judgment: World myth, oral/visual traditions and cross-cultural transmission. Genuine comparative literature, not a substitute for Dutch historical literary studies.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies myth, literary transmission and cultural transformation across historical and global traditions

profiles.name: Life & Travel Writing
profiles.actualContent: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts.
profiles.judgment: Life narratives, memoir/autobiography and critical/creative writing. Genuine literary analysis, not Dutch literary history or publishing practice.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: studies autobiography, travel writing, identity, memory and cultural self-representation

profiles.name: Film & Text
profiles.actualContent: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
profiles.judgment: Film adaptation and literary/film form. Genuine intermedial literary research, not a documented Dutch medium/orality seminar.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: analyses adaptation, intertextuality and cross-media narrative between literature and film

profiles.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
profiles.actualContent: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
profiles.judgment: Humanist/feminist/Marxist/minority/psychoanalytic interpretation and research project. Genuine literary theory and enquiry, not Dutch-specific historical or linguistic depth.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: applies feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic perspectives in a literary research project

profiles.name: Introduction to Film & Media
profiles.actualContent: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
profiles.judgment: Film history, form and cultural analysis; media contribution, not Dutch language or literary historiography.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: develops analysis of film and media as cultural production that shapes identity, power and public meaning

profiles.name: Media Archaeology
profiles.actualContent: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
profiles.judgment: Material history of obsolete media and cultural meaning. Genuine medium/material analysis, not a Dutch literary oral-history sequence.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines print and pre-digital media as material forms that shape cultural memory and communication

profiles.name: From T.V. to TikTok
profiles.actualContent: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.
profiles.judgment: American media narratives, identity, disability and representation. Genuine media/social interpretation, not Dutch/Flemish cultural history.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: examines how television and social media shape attitudes, narratives and public responses

profiles.name: The Documentary
profiles.actualContent: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
profiles.judgment: Documentary history, forms, ethics and short production. Useful multimodal communication, not guaranteed professional broadcasting or Dutch literary research.
profiles.originalTraceClaim: combines documentary analysis with research, argument and production of a short documentary

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: hough transform for detection of lines; detection of corners; self driving vehicles; feature detection; image; processing

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Living with Water
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: Delta regions around the world face growing challenges related to sea-level rise, flooding, freshwater scarcity, land subsidence, and unequal access to water and protection. At the same time, these regions are home to millions of people whose lives are shaped by water. This course explores how societies in delta regions manage water risks and opportunities, with a particular focus on the Dutch province of Zeeland as a living laboratory. Students are introduced to key concepts in sustainable water management, including flood protection, drainage and freshwater management, salinization, land subsidence, the ecological consequences of water infrastructure, and the social dimensions of water governance. The course examines how historical events have shaped contemporary approaches to water management, and how governance structures, laws, and institutions influence decisions about safety, land use, sustainability, and whose interests are prioritized. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the idea of adapting to water dynamics through integrated strategies, nature-based solutions, and resilient planning, while critically reflecting on questions of long-term social impacts. Learning takes place through a combination of assigned readings, short lectures, group discussions, and in-class activities that encourage critical reflection and collaborative learning. Students engage with real-world cases through guest speakers from policy and research, as well as excursions and field-based activities in Zeeland when possible.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: flood protection; freshwater management; land subsidence; ecological consequences of water infrastructure; social dimensions of water governance; highlights nature based

boundedCatalogueScan.name: History Research Seminar
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: many foreign troops like irish; emphasises methodological rigour; substantial research paper; interdisciplinary thinking; engaging critically; historical inquiry

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Psycholinguistics
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Advanced Research Seminar
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: calculate effect sizes; inform evidence-based policy; synthesize results; systematic reviews; really works; combining results
boundedCatalogueScan.methods: Psychological research design; Literature review; Data analysis

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Dutch
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Style & Meaning
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: linguistic choices inform; choices inform meaning; addresses power dynamics; non-fiction contexts; ideological undertones; close reading

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Rhetoric in Action
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: primary school children; local primary school; persuasive speaking; rhetorical theory; voices; public-speaking

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: or digitally mediated work; creative; sonic poetry; unconventional forms; poetic forms; communication

boundedCatalogueScan.name: Film & Text
boundedCatalogueScan.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
boundedCatalogueScan.profile: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
boundedCatalogueScan.topics: interpretive strategies; viewer participation; diverse dynamics between literary text; cultural analysis; modern sociology; visual anthropology
